utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Today, we are Wednesday, March the 4th, 2009. I would like to greet Ms. Biersay, Mr. Mundis, and all their collaborators. I would also like to greet Mr. Seselj, as well as all the other people who are helping us in and around the courtroom. This hearing was not part of the programme at the beginning of the week, and we were not able to hold it because, as you know, this witness was supposed to come a few days ago, but because of his health, because of some health issues, he was not able to come, and we now have the certainty that the person will be able to come and testify, and this is why we have informed Mr. Seselj immediately so that he is aware of the fact the witness was to come today to testify. So as to the decision on the adjournment, this is the last witness who will come to testify. So this is where we are today. Mr. Seselj, would you like to add something before we bring the witness in?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Presiding Judge. I do have something to say. I believe that the Prosecution has to inform both the Trial Chamber and me about the health condition of this witness and the reasons why he did not testify in time. I think that this is very important, and generally speaking I'm not quite sure that he did have health problems. I think that this was a game played by the OTP and that they were actually unsure whether they would call this witness or not, up to the last minute, because the OTP is aware of all the possible consequences of the appearance of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please rest assured that I will put the questions, the necessary questions, to the witness, and I will also ask him to tell us about his health when he is here at the Bar. And I would like to -- and, of course, for that part we will go into private session. And these questions may be of interest to you, so you will obtain a very -- very shortly, you will obtain answers to your queries. Now, please, Mr. Usher, could you please bring the witness in. I would like to remind the Prosecution that they will have one hour for the examination-in-chief, and Mr. Seselj will have as well one hour. This is what the Chamber decided, given the health of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good morning [as interpreted], sir. Before I proceed, I would like to ask you to give us your name, your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alija Gusalic, born on the 3rd of March, 1968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A labourer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you ever testified before a tribunal on facts that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time that you are testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you testified twice. Could you tell us in which cases, if you know, trials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once, it was here, in the case against Mr. Milosevic, and once in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in Tuzla, it was against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Against Fikret, Piklic. Actually, I don't know the surname. The first name is Fikret, and his nickname is Piklic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have more questions for you, but I would like to put them in a private session. Mr. Registrar, could you please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very well. Witness, can you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, just some very brief explanations. You will have to answer to questions that will be put to you by Ms. Biersay. She may also show you some documents, and we've allowed a maximum time of one hour for this. And also during that period of time, the Judges, who are sitting before you, may also put questions to you. Once that -- the questions put by Ms. Biersay are over, Mr. Seselj, who is sitting to your left, will also put some questions as part of a cross-examination, and this is according to the rules and regulations of this Tribunal, and you know how things go because you testified in the Milosevic case, and you know very well, if you will remember that you had to answer questions that were put to you by both parties. So please try to be clear, to be precise, when you give your answers. And if you don't understand a question, please do not hesitate to ask the questioning party to put the question to you again. And if at one point -- some point in time you don't feel very well, please let us -- we are here to assist you as well. This is what I had to say. Ms. Biersay, you have the floor. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another preliminary objection, because the witness stated that at a certain point he had taken the witness stand in a trial in Tuzla. I have no trace of having been submitted this bit of information by the OTP in my papers, so I should like the OTP to tell me whether they have submitted this to me, and if so when, and what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will read from a February 23rd, 2009 letter that we sent to Mr. Seselj, and in that letter we told him: "Today," being the 23rd of February, 2009, "the witness informed the Prosecution that he testified in Tuzla in either 2001 or 2004," more likely 2004. "We have requested the testimony." And that is in a letter that we submitted to Mr. Seselj after we met with the witness in proofing last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But, Ms. Biersay, the Tuzla testimony you don't -- you didn't have it. Did the witness tell you this when you met with him on the 23rd of February; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's correct that we learnt about the Tuzla testimony on the day that we met with the witness, the same day of the letter, February 23rd, 2009, and we have also submitted the formal request for transcripts of that testimony, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, Ms. Biersay's letter, in itself, I do appreciate all of her letters, I'm making a special collection of them, but it cannot substitute documentation on the testimony of this witness. If it was only on the 23rd of February that the Prosecutor learned that this witness had testified in Tuzla, and today is the 4th of March, the OTP did have time to obtain the complete documentation, the complete file from Tuzla, and to submit it to me. Tuzla is not at the end of the world, and I need this for my cross-examination. The Prosecutor does not have time to translate it into English, but they still speak Serbian in Tuzla and I can read it. And please warn the witness -- caution the witness that he can only answer the questions and cannot interfere with our discussions here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, do not interrupt Mr. Seselj when he is speaking. Mr. Seselj, the representative of the OTP told us that when she learned, on the 23rd of February, that the gentleman testified in Tuzla, she sent a letter immediately to the authorities so that the transcript could be sent. She also told us that she did not get the transcript yet. Is that correct, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I think that that is no excuse for the OTP. They could have obtained it by courier. They could have sent their courier to Tuzla, have a photostatic copy of the testimony made and brought to The Hague. What does it mean? We asked for it and we didn't get it. I mean, this is not the first time. Remember Kulic and several other similar witnesses, and I never got those documents later, because once the testimony's over, I mean, the testifying, everything is forgotten. So I insist to be -- obtain this testimony from Tuzla in order for me to be able to use it in my cross-examination. This is my right, and my rights cannot be trampled upon by a simple statement to the effect, "We asked for it and we did not get it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I do not know how things function in Tuzla, how they go in Tuzla, but let's suppose that this is taking place in Paris, and then on the 23rd of February the accused informs Ms. Biersay of this. Ms. Biersay would have informed the French authorities in order to get not a transcript, because we don't have a transcript in France, but to get the judgement or something like that, and, believe me, it would take a few months before she would get the document. And in Italy, it would be probably the same thing; maybe worse. So that's all we have right now. We can say that it's unfortunate, yes, but that's what it is, that's what we have, that's the situation. Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In accordance with the Court's ruling with respect to the time, the one hour, I will ask for some flexibility, Your Honours, in the form that my questions are in, and I will, in advance, tell the Court that I will be skipping certain transitional components of the witness's testimony in order to fit it within the hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusalic, could you tell the members of the Trial Chamber where you were born?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Gornji Sepak, Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you grow up, for the most part?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us where Bijeljina is, in relation to the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It is upstream the Drina River, some four kilometres upstream.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I completed primary school, eight grades. Then for another three years, I went to a civil engineering or construction school. So I went to school for 11 years, and I'm a worker, construction worker.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber the ethnic composition of Bijeljina? Was it one ethnicity more than another?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Muslims, Serbs, and Croats lived in Bijeljina. The majority population in Bijeljina were Muslims, and in the surrounding villages they were Serbs, the majority population. And we got along very well until the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You, yourself, were you married at some point?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was married twice. My first wife was a Serb, and the second one as well, she was also a Serb. And currently, I'm not married.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described to the Trial Chamber that these different ethnicities got along. Did there come a time when that changed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several months before the war broke out, it was disastrous. Everything had changed totally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe in what way things changed?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness sit closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some uniformed and armed people started walking about. That was a couple of months before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who -- how were these people dressed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: These were the people, the Territorial Defence, and the infiltrated Serbs who trained people, reportedly the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The person who held -- in that period that you're now describing, you say before the war, are we talking 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The person who held the position of mayor, do you know what ethnicity that person was, mayor of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I think that he was a Serb. I'm not sure. I was not engaged in politics, so that I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What about the commander of the police; do you know that person's ethnicity, what it was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when there were letters calling up reservists in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only one people, only the Serbs got them. I have three brothers, and I am the fourth, and we didn't get any calls.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you serve any military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, for ten months.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to direct your attention to a village by the name of Amajlije. Where is that village in relationship to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It is some three to four kilometres from Bijeljina, up the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was it on the Republic of Serbia side or on the Bijeljina side?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: The Bijeljina side, up the Drina, upstream the Drina River, because the Drina connects Serbia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What, if any, military training -- in the time-period that you're talking about before the war started in 1992, what type of training do you know, if you know, happened at that -- in that village?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That is in 1992. There was training involving the Arkan's men and Seselj's men from Serbia. They were training the local Serbs in order for them to attack Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know the name of someone called Mirko Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in 1992, at the beginning of 1992, did he have any political affiliations that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seselj actually designated him his vojvoda of the Radical Party, the Radicals.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Specifically in 1992, do you know whether or not Mr. Mirko Blagojevic was a member of the Radical Party in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes? What position, if any, did he hold --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I was checking your age, and in 1992 you were 25 -- 24 years old, 24 years old. So if I'm not mistaken, you were married to a Serb woman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twice, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You've also told us that you were not politically engaged. Tell us, how is it that you knew that a certain person was involved in a certain political party, that another person was involved in another political party? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People talked about it. People talked about who was what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where; is that coffee shop, or on the stadium, or on the street, on television? Where, where could you hear this? At the hairdresser's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, Mr. Seselj spoke out in public, that there was a Radical Party, that he was a Chetnik. And about Mirko Blagojevic? Well, people talked about him in cafes and so on, whereas Mr. Seselj was a politician and he was for the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, if I understand you correctly, in 1992 you had heard of Mr. Seselj, and Mr. Blagojevic was saying that he belonged to Mr. Seselj's party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not Mr. Seselj visited the Bijeljina area in the first part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but he did visit on one occasion, and there was a big rally in Bijeljina in front of the municipal building. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did that happen --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I attended that rally, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did that rally happen before the war started or after the war started?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, going back to Mr. Blagojevic, was he associated in any way with a cafe in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had a cafe called "Srbija." I think it was his, that he was the actual owner of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did that cafe have a different name before the war started? You don't have to tell me the name, but was there another name?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: He used to be called -- it used to be called "Foco," and after that, "Srbija."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How soon before the war was the name changed to Cafe Srbija?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: A few months, I think, but I'm not sure exactly. It was just a few months.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time in Bijeljina, again in that 1992 period that we're discussing, when local Serb men were armed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed. The garrison was theirs, everything was in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what individuals, if any, associated with the Serb Radical Party, participated in the arming of the Serb men in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This is a leading question. The question should be, "Were there persons from the Serb Radical Party also participating in the arming?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you understand the question that I asked?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat it now, please? I was listening to what the general was saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Fair enough. Could you tell me what members of the Serbian Radical Party participated in the arming of local Serb men?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection again. This is now impertinent. It's not "what members," but "did any members." "What members" implies that there certainly were some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, why don't you put a broader question to the witness, such as who was arming -- who was armed, rather, and then -- otherwise it's really leading, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of individuals who were arming local Serb men in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to tell you the names?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Seselj, Arkan, and Mirko Blagojevic among the local people. I know him well, personally. They were the ones arming people. But all of it was from the former Yugoslavia, so all the weapons that the Muslim people, the Croat people, the Serb people, everyone had bought for the former Yugoslavia, they appropriated all that for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to direct your attention to March 1992. Now, I know that a lot happened in March 1992, but what I'd like to ask you about are those events -- immediate events that caused you to be hospitalised. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This question again is impermissible. First let's see what the events in Bijeljina were, what actually happened to the witness, if anything, and not, "Did you end up in hospital because of that?" What sort of question is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness left the hospital, something must have happened, so take it chronologically, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In relation to this event that happened with you being hospitalised, could you describe for the Trial Chamber how it is that you ended up in the hospital in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How would he know or, rather, how would she know? How does Madam Biersay know that he ended up in hospital when he hasn't had the chance to say that in the courtroom? How can she know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 65 ter summary, for example. Your Honour, if he continues to interrupt, this will take longer, and if the Court is willing to shorten his time, then I can certainly ask these questions again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let Ms. Biersay do her job, and during the cross-examination you may ask that question. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you're asking me to tolerate Madam Biersay's leading questions, I'll do that, but then the cross-examination doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay is not going to put leading questions. That is not the problem. Some events took place in Bijeljina, and apparently the witness was the victim of these events, so we have to establish what happened, who did what, were there some people belonging to the Serb Radical Party; if so, who were they and so on. That's what's really important. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, I am concerned about the basis of your knowledge that this witness was a victim in Bijeljina. How do you know he was a victim? The OTP has lied to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. We'll see, we'll see. Let's see, let's establish things. Very well. Ms. Biersay, please proceed step by step. Otherwise, Mr. Seselj will continue to raise objections. If I was carrying out the cross-examination, or, rather, the examination-in-chief, in ten minutes I would solve that problem, but you are putting questions, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm trying to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusalic, could you describe to the Trial Chamber when it was that you were shot in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do we know that he was shot, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Biersay, are you doing it on purpose or not? All the questions you are putting are leading. All you have to do is just say, "Tell us, sir, in March, what happened?" And then he will tell you, "Somebody shot at me in March." And then you take on and you continue. Do you understand, Ms. Biersay, or not? You stem of the common law system, so you know very well that when it comes to leading questions, you may put them, but in a very delicate way. You have to avoid asking leading questions during the examination-in-chief. So you can ask the question of the witness, what he was doing in the month of March 1992, and then he can explain to you that there was an attack, and then you can start asking questions about various details. Otherwise, Mr. Seselj is not going to stop. As soon as you put a leading question, he will raise an objection. So once again, I would like to remind you. Personally, I think that this witness could have been a 92 bis witness. I do not understand the position of the Prosecution to, at all costs, bring this witness. You might have reasons that I don't know of. And we also know how the witness is feeling. We should not really stress him out too much. And we also know very well that he came to testify according to a guide-line, and knowing very well what happened in Bijeljina, and that's all we have in our minds. So please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: As the Court is aware, I have one hour in which to do the examination. I'm trying to be very focused. I have previously met with this witness and asked him what happened in 1992, and there's a lot that happened in 1992. So for the Court's benefit and for Mr. Seselj's benefit, I am trying to be as focused as possible. Mr. Seselj has repeatedly interrupted me, and it's a very simple question with respect to this witness. I am trying to jump over certain events to get to what I think the Trial Chamber is interested in hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Have you ever been in the hospital in Bijeljina as a patient?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was wounded on the 31st of March, 1992, at 0815 hours when the Chetniks shot at us, the Radicals, in front of Cafe Srbija.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you were doing or trying to do at the time that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I wanted to throw a hand-grenade into Cafe Srbija.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you try to do that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I had been in Cafe Srbija an hour before, and downstairs they were all armed, Seselj's men, Arkan's men, Mirko's men, ready to attack Bijeljina. They were going to occupy it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber why you decided to go to Cafe Srbija with the -- was it a bomb or a hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It was a hand-grenade, hand-grenade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Witness, you had this hand-grenade before, when you went to Cafe Srbija? When you understood that they were going to attack Bijeljina, did you already have the hand-grenade, or did you obtain it afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I obtained it. There are two cafes. One was Srbija, the other one was Istanbul. They were some 50 or 60 metres away from each other. A few days before that, a hand-grenade had been thrown into Cafe Istanbul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question. How did you understand, when you went to Cafe Srbija, how did you understand that the people there were Arkan's men, Seselj's men, Blagojevic's men, that they were ready to attack Bijeljina? From what did you gather that impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived in Cafe Srbija, there were two guards standing outside in camouflage uniform with rifles. I think that was proof enough. When I went down there, it was chalk full, it was crowded with armed men. I could tell that they were Arkan's men and Seselj's men because they spoke with different accents than we did. Their accents were those that people from Serbia had, and I knew [indiscernible]. I had grown up there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter is not sure of the last name mentioned by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how long did you stay hospitalised after you were shot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I thought that Ms. Biersay was going to ask you some questions that I actually had in mind. First of all, talk to us about that hand-grenade. Where did you go and get it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Cafe Istanbul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand correctly, you were 24 years old, you were married to a Serb woman, and you see some people in a cafe, and then you get this idea to go to Cafe Istanbul to go get a hand-grenade in order to throw it in the Cafe Srbija; is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because a hand-grenade had been thrown into Cafe Istanbul, and there was civilians in there. Serbs, Muslims, everyone visited the Cafe Istanbul. In Cafe Srbija, there were armed men inside. There were no civilians there. They were the people who wanted to do what they did in the former -- or, rather, the present Bosnia. They made a massacre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you wanted to revenge, because what had happened at Cafe Istanbul? You decided to act alone and to go and to throw a hand-grenade in Cafe Srbija as a retaliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Because I had been in the cafe, and when I was there, Mirko Blagojevic told me that I was not wanted there in that cafe. I asked him, Why? Is it because I'm a Muslim? And he said, I didn't say that. And then I left, and those armed men remained there in the cafe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So it was in order to prevent the attack on Bijeljina that you expected; was that the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it could be. Yes, you could say that, because had I thrown the hand-grenade into the cafe, the Chetniks who had arrived in Bijeljina and in Bosnia from Serbia might have been killed, I might have been killed too, but the other people, the population, would have been left in peace, and they could have continued their lives normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if we understand correctly, you throw the hand-grenade, somebody shoots you, and then you're injured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, well, I don't understand anything anymore, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not throw the hand-grenade into the cafe. I didn't succeed in my intention, because some 15 or 10 metres away from the cafe, they shot me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were at a distance of 15 metres, but were you inside the cafe or outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In front of the cafe, before I reached it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you were outside. So when they saw you come, they shot you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you fall to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. My horse also fell, because I was riding a horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you were riding a horse, but nothing happened to the horse. You fell from the horse, and nobody came to help you? You were just left there injured on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shooting started. The horse was wounded. I never found it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Who brought you to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was when both sides started shooting. I managed to get out, and a man took me to hospital in his car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Ms. Biersay, so now we're at the hospital. You can take it from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how many days did you stay in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Nine days, a whole nine days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to -- did anyone come into the hospital that mistreated you in any way?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who mistreated you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: The hospital -- well, it was the hospital. The shooting had already started, but the hospital was in the hands of the Muslims for the first two or three days. After that, it was occupied by the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were mistreated while you were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. First of all, Madam Biersay asks who mistreated him in the hospital. The witness says that the hospital was in Muslim hands, and then two or three days later the Chetniks arrived. And then she asks, "Who mistreated you in the hospital," and the witness did not confirm that he was mistreated. If you find this acceptable, I won't object anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm directing the Court to page 28, line 2. "Q. Did anyone come to the hospital that mistreated you in any way? "A. Yes." Now that he has said that he was mistreated, I'd like him to answer the question about who mistreated him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber who mistreated you in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That response was not given in the Serbian language here. The transcript is your affair, but the witness was clear. He said that he was in the hospital, the hospital was in Muslim hands for three days, and that the Chetniks then arrived. He didn't say a word about mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you spent three days in the hospital, and the hospital was in the hands of the Chetniks, so you were mistreated after those three days? No? Well, could you please explain, then. When you were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't spend three days in the hospital, I spent nine days there. For three days, the hospital was in Muslim hands. After the fall of the hospital, when the Chetniks took it over, that's when the mistreatment began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Now it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who mistreated you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Shall I tell you the name or --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The name, yes.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic, with two others.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber how he mistreated you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: He broke the infusion tubes, the drip tubes, and then he stuck something into my wound. He said he would come back to vent his feelings on me. He mentioned the village of Amajlije.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did he say about the village of Amajlije, Mirko Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: He said that whoever had been taken there had never come back alive. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber whether or not the hospital was visited by any known politicians?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: President Ms. Plavsic, Fikret Abdic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After Mirko Blagojevic put something in your wound, as you described it to the Trial Chamber, did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. When Fikret and Ms. Plavsic arrived, he was the man leading the group. He came there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you or do anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Do you mean in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, in the hospital. Did he say anything to you during the time that he was with the other people you mentioned, Plavsic, Abdic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: He said that all this had been done by para-armies and that the JNA would arrive and calm things down, and that's what happened in the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please, and come a bit closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which of these three people told him that. I don't see that. JUDE ANTONETTI: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Witness, who told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Plavsic and Abdic said that. They were in a group all together and they were all talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When were you -- how is it that you came to be released from the hospital after the nine days that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Arkan, Arkan had me discharged. He said that I was to go home, that nobody would touch me. But he also said that I was not to leave my home at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Would you describe that as some kind of house arrest, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: What it was was waiting for them to come and slaughter me. That is what it was, to slit my throat. I was released from there, but told not to go anywhere; stay put.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you stay at home?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After the while that you just described, why did you leave home?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, I received a letter which scared me, and I fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did the letter say that scared you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It was just a couple of sentences. It said: "Turk, the time has come for you to pay for what you have done to us." I don't know what it was that I had done to them, and it was signed: "Chetniks," because those who wrote that letter did not want to actually sign their actual names, so it was just signed, "Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you arrested after you left your home?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, after some time, after some time. I'm not sure how much time after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: The allegedly civilian police then, the MUP, which at the time was supposed to be good for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was that the only time that you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No. I was caught then, and then I spent some time there - I'm not sure how much - and then I managed to escape from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "time there," do you mean the MUP, you were kept at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And after you escaped from the MUP, you were again arrested at a later time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, after a month or two, or, rather, a month and a half. I do not know the exact date, but that was about the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who arrested you on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They were masked, in uniform and masked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you taken when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: To the MUP again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being arrested this time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me anything. They just hit me, and nobody asked me anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how long were you kept at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Four days, which seemed like four years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On the fourth day, did any other prisoners join you at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, three of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was their ethnic background, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They were also Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the names of those three people?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Ejup Smajic, Zlatar, and Ferid Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How were they treated at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They were treated exactly the way I was. Nobody asked us anything. They just kept hitting us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After your fourth day at the MUP, were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They put some stockings or some bags on our heads, and they told us that they were taking us to Amajlije.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before they put the stockings or bags on your heads, were you able to see what kind of vehicle you were going to be put in?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who else was taken with you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Ejup Smajic, Zlatar - I'm not sure of his name - and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you talking about the same three people who were brought into the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And were you, in fact, taken to Amajlije, like you had been told you were going to be?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No. They drove us to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe for the Trial Chamber what that Batkovic camp looked like once you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It consisted of two hangars. People would be placed in either. There was a barbed wire fence. There were two guardhouses. They drove the people inside. There were two tents outside, because not all the people could fit into the two hangars, so there were these two tents outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How long were you kept at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: The first time, for about three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: During those three months, were you able to estimate approximately how many prisoners were being kept there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: About 2.000, give a take a few, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber the approximate period of time that you were there? What months of 1992, the first time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I think it was June or July. I know that it was very hot.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Going back to the approximate number that you just described for the Trial Chamber, of those people, were you able to tell what the ethnic composition was of the 2.000 people?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They were predominantly Muslims, most of them were Muslims. There were a few Croats, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: During your first -- the first stay, the three months you just described, could you -- did you come to learn from what villages some of those people came from?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Which villages? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Vlasenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Brcko, Brezovo Polje, Kalesija, Tojcici. There were many places. Actually, there were people from different places, all over.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And just to orient the Trial Chamber, where is Batkovic compared to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It is some five or six kilometres away from Bijeljina, in the opposite direction from where Amajlije is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you were there for the first time, "there" being Batkovic, the Batkovic camp, did you see any elderly prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few elderly people, and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What about women?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: There was one woman.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Of these approximately 2.000 people, were you able to estimate how many of them were civilians and how many of them were not civilians?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They were all civilians. There were perhaps two prisoners whom they called "Green Berets." All the rest were civilians and infirm/helpless people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the camp -- the Batkovic camp was?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It was a warrant officer from Novi Sad, but I've forgotten his name again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before, you described this -- that you believe the approximate start of your detention was in June of 1992, and you described how very hot it was. Could you tell the members of the Trial Chamber if anyone died because of the conditions in the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And approximately how many people died from the conditions of the camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: About a hundred of them, and a large number also, perhaps ten of them, succumbed to the beating. Of the three men who came with me, two succumbed to the beating, died from the beatings, Zlatar and Ferid Zecevic. They were killed, and I and Ejup Smajic survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you beaten while you were in the Batkovic camp during those three months?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How often were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Five times a day, and sometimes more than that. It was breakfast, lunch, dinner, lining up, and then hitting us at night as much as they possibly could.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It would be better if you asked me what they -- what they didn't beat us with.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But could you give some examples of what they -- what they used?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Chains, sticks, handles, axe handles. They tested all of that on us, and then eventually they would use stones, and I had to kneel to make it possible for them or easier for them to hit me with stones.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why did you have to kneel?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Because they were small people and not exactly brawny, and I was a big one, and they were unable to hit me in the head when I was -- while I was standing on my feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What injuries did you get from all that beating?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Fractures. My ribs were broken, two on this side, three on this side [indicates]. My arm was broken, my back. I have eight stitches on my head. And there is more. Some of it is still visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What food, if any, would you get during those three months?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Just some beans, bean soup that had already gone bad. How could you eat it? I didn't even eat it. They would beat me and then just give me something to eat, like to a dog.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The people who were beating you, what ethnicity were they, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were they --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: And, regrettably, they were -- there were also two Muslims who also beat the prisoners. Why did they do that? To save their own skin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you ever mistaken for being dead during the first three months that you were detained at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of a question is this, Judges? Did the accused [as interpreted] ever think that he was dead? These questions are senseless. How can the witness think himself dead?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That was not the question, and I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did other people believe that you were dead because --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, it is the interpreter's mistake, and I withdraw my objection, because what the interpreter had said was whether the witness had thought himself dead. That's why I objected, and I withdraw my objection, Madam Biersay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake in interpretation. Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, could you please elicit also with the witness if he is able to inform us about who the Serb prison guards were; JNA soldiers, volunteers, or any identification that the witness is able to give us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber how it is that other people thought you were dead?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I was taken out four times with the dead. As they were taking us out, I would move a leg or an arm, and then they would say, This one is alive, and then they would take me back. And this happened four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, before I turn your attention to the question that Judge Harhoff posed, could you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not you were put in a certain group while you were in the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were always ten of us in a group, which they called "the specials." Now, what they considered specials, I don't know. Perhaps that we were specially reserved for beatings. Maybe that was why they called us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the question of -- are you able to describe the uniforms, for example, that the people who were beating you -- the non-prisoners who were beating you, do you remember any of those uniforms that the people beating you wore?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: There were different uniforms. There was the uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army, there were camouflage uniforms, black uniforms which the -- which the local Serbs calling themselves "Arkan's men" wore. There were all manner of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: During the time that you were detained during the -- the first time at the Batkovic camp, did the ICRC ever visit that camp in the three months that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you ever registered with the ICRC during the first three months you were kept at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They did not register me and these other nine specials. They did register the elderly and the children, but we were hidden. We would be taken a kilometre or two away from the hangar. So they would always be informed when the ICRC would come, and then they would hide us before they came.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you mistreated in any way while you were hidden from the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, the ten of us would always be separated, and they took us to this facility where they used to keep their cattle before, which was called the "Cardak" [phoen], and they did all sorts of things, unimaginable things, something that would never occur to a normal person, to us while they kept us in that facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. This camp, the Batkovici camp, I'm looking at these documents, but we don't see any mention of that camp. And in the brief, we see, in the footnote, two or three times -- but I'm talking about the brief. I'm not talking about the statement. In the brief, the witness -- of the witness, it is said, with respect to the occupation of the city, on the footnote 238, it is said that the volunteers circled and attacked Bijeljina. It is also said, on footnote 241, with regard to the participation of Blagojevic, that he took part in various assaults. And it is also said, on footnote 244, as regards Cafe Srbija, where Mr. Seselj would have come to that Cafe Srbija. That's all we see. So you spent almost one hour talking about the camp, whereas in the indictment and in the brief, it is not mentioned at all. You can do whatever you wish, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: As the Court is aware, we are presenting this evidence to show the pattern of crimes, and I understand that this is not specifically alleged in the indictment, and this is a dropped crime site, as the Court is aware. So the testimony is meant to show patterns of the crimes committed, as we stated. And if I could direct the Court to the 65 ter summary, there was -- these events are described therein. Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock, and I'm not sure if the Court would prefer to take a break --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something. Just may I be allowed to say something before the break? Mr. President, because we have been informed that there is a doctor present in the courtroom, I demand that during this break the present physician examine the legs of this witness. On one of his legs, I suppose it is his left leg, he should have a scar from a gun-shot -- or, rather, a pistol wound. We would like the doctor to tell us that, whether in addition to that pistol wound, there is a bayonet scar, bayonet wound scar. This is something that can be easily ascertained by any physician by just a visual examination. A wound from a bayonet can heal, but it cannot but leave a visible scar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, it's an interesting request, but procedurally speaking, the doctor does almost nothing. In other words, this is a doctor who either makes certificates or he can also give an injection, but he is not a treating physician. If we ask him to do so, he will definitely refuse to come and examine the witness in this fashion. Now, you told us, Witness, that you were beaten, your bones were broken. Do you have on your leg a scar of a bayonet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it visible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... wounded, and it is visible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is confusing the wound, pistol wound, and a stab by a bayonet. He's confusing these two. Perhaps it wasn't interpreted correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you told us that when you were at the hospital, while you were there, Mirko Blagojevic came with his bayonet, and then he stabbed you with his bayonet, he put the bayonet inside your wound. Was it that same wound at your leg? Did he put the bayonet inside or did he just sort of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... stabbed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see. Did he pierce your skin, did he cut through your leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was wounded, the bullet exited the wound, so I was first shot and there was an entry and exit wound, and then he stabbed me in that wound, precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when we talk about an entry and exit wound on the leg, if the artery has not been hit, there is no surgical intervention. The wound is just externally dressed, and it heals very quickly. So a scar -- a scar from a pistol wound --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, my colleague is right, it is something that you may put during your cross-examination. You will have the opportunity to do so while you cross-examine. So at present, right now, actually, we can only conclude that the witness was injured, and we can conclude that he told us that Blagojevic put a bayonet through his wound. That's all. Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Very quickly, I want to make the record that the witness, in this courtroom, never said "bayonet." Mr. Seselj is using items from the statement, injecting it, and then creating a false issue. That is the subject of cross-examination. But the bayonet was mentioned for the first time by Mr. Seselj in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is simply not true. I have jotted down that the witness mentioned the bayonet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, you're making a mistake, unless I'm completely mistaken, but I thought -- I thought I heard that the witness told us that while he was at the hospital, Mr. Blagojevic took a bayonet and stabbed him in the wound. So, Witness, you are the only person who can really shed some light on this. Did you actually say that Mr. Blagojevic put his bayonet in your wound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether it was a knife or a bayonet, to my mind, that is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So a bayonet or a knife, for you it's the same thing. Very well. Let's take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you taken after the three months of detention at the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: To Doboj, to a small camp there at Usora in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was that a camp like the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, it was smaller than that, with fewer people in it, but it also consisted of hangars.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And were you kept as a prisoner there in that camp as well?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we were beaten less.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how long were you at the camp in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Eleven and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did that camp have another name?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Usora.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In addition to being beaten as well at that camp, were prisoners made to do any forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What kind of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: All kinds of work that a man can do, from chopping wood, working in warehouses, digging trenches, pulling out dead Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "pulling out dead Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: When there was shooting when there were clashes, we would pull out the dead. Some Chetniks, others Muslims, so my answer was not entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where was it that you pulled out --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: In the surrounding villages, at the front-lines around Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that true for both -- you used the word "Chetniks." Was that true for Chetniks as well as Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: The dead, yes, those who were dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After being detained in Doboj, were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took us back to Batkovic because of some big exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how long did you spend in Batkovic for the second time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When were you finally released?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how do you consider that day, November 8th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It's another birthday for me, a second birthday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you, Ms. Biersay. Just one additional question to the witness. You said, very quickly, that Mr. Seselj held a rally in March 1992, that's what I understood, in Bijeljina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said before the war broke out in Bijeljina, which was before March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what year; 1990, 1991, 1989? Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said "1992."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992, before the war broke out, 1991 or 1992, a few months -- three months before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And you told us that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It started in Bijeljina on the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was before. And did you go to that rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All the citizens went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody was there, and Mr. Seselj also --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the citizens, yes. He made speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you listen to his speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I listened for a while, and then I left. Later on, a fight broke out, as I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after that, there was a fight, a fight. Now, this is getting interesting. So there was a fight between whom and whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a fight between Serbs and Muslims. He made them quarrel by his speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was the police there or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was a normal situation at the time. There was no war in Bosnia as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So it wasn't the war yet. So if what you are saying is true, and I am insisting on the "if," if indeed this rally took place, this speech was held, whether you know it or not, at the time, in order to hold a political rally, did one have to ask an authorisation from the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had all of that in his hands. He went wherever he wanted to go and did whatever he wanted to do. He held it all in his hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. And you said, "I went to the rally, I did not stay."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... but I didn't stay there until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And you were absolutely certain it was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a few months before, either 1991 or 1992. It was either in late 1991 or early 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] End of 1991, early 1992. You don't remember. You also don't remember how you were dressed? Did you wear a coat, did you wear jeans, did you wear something warmer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Were there any reporters there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... me? What do I know? Yes, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to your knowledge, were there any press releases afterwards about the meeting, any articles as to the meeting? Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told the gentlemen that I was no politician and I didn't read that, but of course it was broadcast on television as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be able to explain to us, why is it that of all the witnesses that were heard on -- who were heard on Bijeljina, nobody mentioned that rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they're afraid, and they all went there in hiding, but I'm not afraid because I never, ever want to go back to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that they were fearing something. I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... anymore, but those people there are afraid to speak out, they're afraid to say anything. I love my country, Bosnia, I love my people, but there's no place for me there anymore, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you remember if, during the rally, if it was spring-time, was it winter-time? How were people dressed; do you remember? Was there any snow on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the weather was normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it could have been spring or early spring? Could it have been between winter and spring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea. How do I know what the weather was like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But if you don't remember, you don't have to remember it. I'm just asking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have one hour. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gusalic, do you still live in Iowa, in the USA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That's not your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You should address me politely.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't have to speak to you politely, and neither do you have to speak politely to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note it is impossible to interpret overlapping speakers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell him he has no right to ask him [as interpreted] where I live. I would like to ask the Court that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj has the right to cross-examine you and to challenge everything you have said. We know that you do not live in the Netherlands, and the rest is not very important. Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Seselj has not shown any relevance for this question. If we are going to go into the whereabouts of this witness, where he lives, I would request that we do that in closed session. But my first argument is that it's completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, this is not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you still live in the state of Iowa in the USA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm living in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Bijeljina? When did you leave Iowa? You have to answer that question. When did you leave the state of Iowa in the USA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: When I divorced my wife, after the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You also broke American laws?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Don't comment on that. Address me with a polite plural form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you didn't hear that, Your Honours. The witness said, "Well, you see how you know that," addressing me with the singular "you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, don't say "tu," "you" to the accused. He's using the plural, so use the same plural, because he's using the "vous," and this is just to show that you respect him. It's a mark of respect. You understood. Yes, you can proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you come into conflict with American laws while staying in the USA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Not in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You received a court order prohibiting you from coming within a certain distance of your ex-wife, a court injunction, a restraining order, because you maltreated your wife?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you broke the injunction and were arrested. After that, the police found you drunk driving; is that correct? And that's why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer, because the interpreters cannot interpret the answers when there's no pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, once again we run into the problem that the interpreters are unable to follow what you say, each of you, because there's overlap between question and answer, and that makes it impossible for the translators to follow you. And if the translators cannot follow you, then we cannot follow you either. So please make an effort, both of you, and especially you, Mr. Seselj, because you are well accustomed to the system here. Do not put your question before you are sure that the translation of his answer has been completed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the American newspapers also write about your arrests?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of the journal "Cityview" published in Des Moines?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't read English, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What's the name of the town where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't remember. Very well. But you were arrested for drunk driving, for breaking a restraining order from coming close to your ex-wife, and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you ever convicted of a misdemeanor in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have information that in 1990 and 1991 alone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, can you speak louder, because the interpreters have problems hearing you. Please come closer to the microphone and speak louder. Cross-examination is a very difficult moment. You have just come to realise that, because Mr. Seselj is talking about your private life and he seems to have a lot of information. So as you can see, it's a very difficult moment, so please be calm and answer the question. Mr. Seselj, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've just said that you have never been convicted for a petty offence, for a misdemeanor, in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: What do you mean under "petty offence"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That you were before a misdemeanors magistrate.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: You are saying that I killed somebody, slaughtered someone?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
