utterances.text: No. You don't go before an examining magistrate for that. According to my information, in 1990s -- in 1991, you were convicted of a misdemeanor three times.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Just once. That was in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my official information, you were convicted or punished, and, mind you, I'm not interested in 1987, just the 1990s. So in 1990, on the 26th of February, the decision number is 755/90, you violated the public law and order law, and you were punished because of a physical assault on another person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, "vous" with a "tu," the singular you, if you say so, then it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I say it's correct. I have an official document.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then on the 1st of August, 1990, the number is 600, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, I believe you're to repeat what you've already said, i.e., you do not have this document; is that what you were going to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I'd like to make a record of it. Thank you. Could I ask for a copy of it, at this time, from Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, Mr. Seselj told us a few weeks ago it might not be -- it might not have been you, but maybe one of your colleagues. He said that he asked the authorities get some information about the situation -- the criminal records of a whole set of witnesses, and he showed us a B/C/S document in which -- in this document, the authorities gave information for each witness concerning the various offences, with the record number, and I presume Mr. Seselj is reading this document. Is that it, Mr. Seselj, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. Presiding Judge, this is another document. This document refers exclusively to this witness, and that should have been found by Madam Biersay, and that is why I'm not giving her this. But she can check by telephone, referring to these numbers, whether these convictions were indeed made on account of misdemeanors involving violations of public law and order. It was Madam Biersay's duty to obtain these, not mine. I'm not going to assist her, especially not now, after this interruption in the proceedings. I'm not going to assist her in this way. It is not my duty to do so. I have established that in just these two years before the war, he was convicted of a misdemeanor two or three times for violating the public law and order, and his body is full of scars because he was in brawls on a daily basis, fighting daily, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness does not confirm, do you believe we can take your words as being the truth, or would it not be better for you to give us the document, translate it in English, so that we have something to use? I cannot automatically believe in what you're saying if the witness cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Lattanzi, you must know -- you must know that I don't expect you to believe anything that I say. I'm not really trying to convince you that I'm telling the truth. First, the witness did confirm that he had been convicted in 1990. That's in response to my first question. To my second question, he said, "Yes, it is so, if you say so." That's what he responded to me. A third piece of information which I have also refers to a conviction for a misdemeanor. We shall see what the witness will have to say. I know that you have come here with a predetermined concept, that you know in advance how this process will end, no matter what my cross-examination will be like. That is why I'm not trying hard. What is important for me is that the public should see that I have refuted the entire testimony of this witness, and then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do not deserve any answer from me, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I do not agree with what you have said. I am speaking for myself. I'm not speaking on behalf of my colleagues. I'm speaking for myself. I'm in a trial and I'm trying to understand what happened at the time. I'm trying to assess what the witness said. I'm listening to the Prosecutor, and I'm listening to the accused. That's it. And it's based on all that that I will be able to make up my own mind. I thought I understood, because you showed us the first document, that the second document you have in your hands is a document coming from some authority, giving you information about the past history of the witness. Even if we accept that he has -- he's responsible for some petty offences, prior petty offences, nevertheless he is a witness. So please proceed now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am showing here, through my questions, that the witness's answers -- what the conduct of this witness in Bijeljina had been like before that incident which took place outside Srbija Cafe. It is obvious from his entire dossier that he was involved in countless brawls and fights, that he was known for his asocial behaviour. That is my thesis. But you keep interrupting me, and I have the impression that the Trial Chamber does not like the efficiency of my cross-examination, that they do not like the effects that I'm achieving, and I assert that the entire testimony -- I put it to you that the entire testimony of this witness is false, and I'm trying to prove that, but you keep intervening. Madam Biersay should have obtained this in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, nobody wants to interrupt you, but, Mr. Seselj, what I'm telling you, looking at you right in the eyes, if you ever -- if there's anything that leads you to believe that you cannot trust me, just make a request, if you have the slightest impression that I am going in this direction. Otherwise, you can proceed. You can impeach.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President -- Mr. President, as if I were that naive a person, as if it were possible to find anyone at this Tribunal who is better than you. Mr. President, you let me speak in this courtroom, in contrast to others, who jump to their feet in rage whenever I ask for the floor. But I do have this critical attitude towards the Trial Chamber, particularly in respect of your colleagues. But I'm not going to ask for the recusation of any of you, because I think that all of the rest would be worse than you and your colleagues. That is my experience here. I'm not going to ask for any recusations, but on the other hand I will always openly say what I think in a very decent tone, a courteous tone, without any offensive expressions, and I expect that you will listen to something which may be unpleasant but that I feel have to say. So please allow me to proceed with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 20th of May, 1991, were you, by a decision of the Misdemeanors Court in Bijeljina, number 7875, were you convicted for a misdemeanor involving a violation of public law and order for especially impertinent conduct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: You said a couple of minutes ago that I was lying. I've never lied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't tell you that you were lying. It is one thing when I tell the Trial Chamber that you are lying, but in addressing you, I never said that you were lying, and these are two different things which you have to appreciate. I understand that you have problems with understanding some things. I can see that from some other indicators in your biography, but this is something you have to understand. When I address you, I never use any offensive terms. It is my right to give the Trial Chamber a general qualification of your testimony in my view, and you must bear that in mind. So, tell me, is this true?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, fine. Do you know that a criminal report was filed against you and that you were tried, together with another 160 persons, Muslims who participated in these war events in Bijeljina in 1992; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. This is the first time I hear it from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Centre for Public Security in Bijeljina, the 18th of May, 1995, filed a criminal report with the Municipal Public Prosecutor, with 161 people in the file, and you are in place 161, and on the basis of that report, there was an indictment? You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That is -- that is not -- that was not a recognised state.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it is a recognised state. Judges, the OTP should have obtained this document also and should have given it to me rather than have me look for it because all these documents concern this witness and his testimony. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, why didn't you keep me when I was arrested by you, if I was convicted of these things?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look, I'm asking you questions, and I shouldn't answer your questions. You should answer mine. There was something which surprised me in today's examination-in-chief. You said that you had completed eight grades of elementary school and then a construction school after that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, three years of construction school after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So construction school. Civil engineering school is what you completed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my information, it was only primary school that you finished.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, I only have a few exams to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you didn't actually go to school, but you took some exams?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, that is not what you said. You said that you had finished primary school and three years of construction school after that. According to my information, you didn't finish any kind of a construction school. After primary school, you did not pursue any other education.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a construction school, and for joiners, for woodworkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have some data regarding to your education. I'm not going to disclose all of it, because we will have to move into closed session, but I can see that you had all Cs or Ds, except for physical education. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of course, yes, of course. You can see that I looked into all of these things. Witness, you are good, you are good.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You see, I looked into all of that. You said in your statement, which you gave to the Prosecutor in The Hague in 1997, in the first paragraph: "I completed elementary school when I was around 15 years of age." You never mention any secondary construction school, but you say: "My father and my brothers are construction workers, and it is from them that I learned this trade." So there was no construction school. Why did you have to come up and make up one today?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the speakers please not overlap. The interpreter did not hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said today that you saw me in Bijeljina, holding a rally of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Witness, your answer was not heard and recorded. Mr. Seselj asked you whether you went to a construction school, so you have to answer. Whether it's "yes" or "no," but we need an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did complete it. This is the -- a construction -- rather, a course, a course for construction and joiners, construction workers and joiners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it a school or a course?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It was a course, so I completed normally elementary school and then subsequently attended this construction school for construction workers and joiners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You never mentioned in your statement a construction school. You say that your father and your brothers were construction workers, and that from them you learned the trade. You never referred to a school.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It should be there, it should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it is not in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It should be there, it should state where I completed that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's move on. You said that you attended a rally of the Serbian Radical Party held by me in Bijeljina several months prior to the war; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the war, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you there was no meeting at all of the Radical Party in Bijeljina before the war. The first meeting in Bijeljina I held in 1993, in the spring, outside the municipal building, and you were not there.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Outside the department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wait, wait a minute. In the statement which you gave to the OTP of The Hague in 1997, second page, last paragraph, you say: "I know Vojislav Seselj from television, but I have never seen him in Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I never personally talked to him like now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, this is what you stated: "... but I have never seen him in Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But that is page 2nd [as interpreted] of your statement, the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It's not written down well, then, it was not noted properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was not noted properly. And you said that there was a fight at that rally also?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One of the previous witnesses talk about a brawl in Mali Zvornik in 1991, so now it seems that there was a brawl, a fight, at every meeting of the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That's the way you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That's nice, if that's the way we were. Let's go on. You also referred to a hand-grenade which was thrown into the Istanbul Cafe?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I asked you many different questions on this famous rally a while ago, because this question is -- this issue is very important. It is mentioned in Article 22 of the indictment, and it raises a major problem, as far as I'm concerned. You said a while ago, under oath, and I asked you a whole bunch of questions, and I asked you whether you were absolutely sure that you went to this March 1992 meeting in Bijeljina, and you said, "Yes." And you gave us many details concerning the fight afterwards, et cetera. I had seen that in your 1997 statement, you had not mentioned this. Therefore, I ask you a question: What does that mean? Are you sure of what you're saying or you really don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember well, but not in March 1992. It was before March. In March, the conflict broke out in Bijeljina, so it was a couple of months before those events, in late 1991 and early 1992, several months before that, because he went through all of Bosnia, holding rallies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, but not in 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you were preparing the ground for your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, if it was proven that Mr. Seselj never went to Bijeljina in 1992 and 1991, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can you say that it wasn't when it was, that he didn't when he did? And I know that personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, fine. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said here that a hand-grenade had been thrown into Cafe Istanbul?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember who threw the grenade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: A guy from Dvorovi. His name was Goran or Zoran or something. I only know that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But according to official information of the MUP in Bijeljina, the hand-grenade was thrown by Aleksandar Zekic, called Andalaga, as --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: From Dvorovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you said Goran from Dvorovi, and the name is Aleksandar and the surname is Zekic and his nickname is Andalaga, from Dvorovi, and this was some ten days prior to the eruption of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: A couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At least ten days. So the chief of the SUP, the chief of the police in Bijeljina, Predrag Jesuric, did you hear about him?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is a Serb, the chief of the police in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He arrested this Andalaga, Aleksandar Zekic, and took him to Tuzla. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Tuzla, the Muslims were always not only the majority but were also dominant because throughout the war Tuzla was never in Serbian hands. It was in Muslim hands; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So ten days before the war, Predrag Jesuric, the chief of the police, acted according to standard procedure, quite normally, accepted the Serb who had thrown the grenade and sent him to Tuzla to the Regional Correctional Centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That is what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But is it true? You just confirmed it's true?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. You said that in that incident, some Muslims were wounded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: There were both Muslims and Serbs. Seven people were wounded in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember what Serb was wounded on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Goran Vasilic, known as Kriska?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a well-known basketball player; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he was wounded in the Istanbul Cafe on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So both Serbs and Muslims went to Cafe Istanbul. So this man threw a hand-grenade into the cafe and wounded both Serbs and Muslims. After that, he was arrested and convicted and served his sentence in Republika Srpska. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know that a girl was wounded there? Her name was Sofija. She was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that girl, Sofija, a Serb wounded by the hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the hand-grenade wounded both Serbs and Muslims. The thrower of the hand-grenade was arrested, sent to Tuzla, tried, and served a prison sentence; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I wasn't interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the OTP should have been interested in this and investigated it. Very well. Now you are saying or, rather, speaking of an incident that occurred in front of Cafe Srbija. Are you aware that this cafe was on the ground floor and that it was on two levels; there was another cafe in the basement? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware of the name of the cafe in the basement?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It used to be called "Foco." At that time, it was called "Srbija".

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, "Srbija" was the name of the cafe that was on ground level, on the ground floor, that was Cafe Srbija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, it's all one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were two cafes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, it was all one cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The cafe in the basement was called "Marlboro," and it was held by a Muslim who is a friend of Mirko Blagojevic. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't know about that; very well. All right, if you didn't know. When you set out riding your horse to throw a hand-grenade, who gave you the hand-grenade in Cafe Istanbul?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: A friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Goga.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Coso was with him, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know Coso as well?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they gave you a hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you mounted a horse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Don't mention Coso's name. The man is dead, so now is not the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he was with Gogo [phoen] when you got the bomb?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: The hand-grenade. I got it from Gogo, not from Coso.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was Coso there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, he was in the cafe, but he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, according to my information, the two of them were in the cafe. It doesn't matter which of them put the hand-grenade into your hands. I'm not going to deal with Coso here. But you took the hand-grenade, mounted a horse, and galloped towards Cafe Srbija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you swung out your hand with a hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbs standing in front of Cafe Srbija saw you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, the armed ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Mirko Blagojevic personally was there; right? Was Mirko Blagojevic himself there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: There was more than one man there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic pulled out his pistol and fired at you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They fired rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you were hit by one bullet from a pistol in the leg?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, a hundred people came to the camp, claiming to be the one who had wounded me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you were hit only with one bullet?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it came from a pistol?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it came from. It's the doctors who know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the bullet came from a pistol, and it caused an entry-exit wound in your leg?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I wasn't at all interested what weapon was used to fire it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You threw a hand-grenade, but you forgot to pull out the pin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I didn't manage to throw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it landed in front of the cafe. Where was the hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It fell. It fell down when I fell from the horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It fell in front of the cafe, but you didn't have time to pull out the pin?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It fell down on the ground, but not in front of the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know you had to pull the pin out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters cannot follow you. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic pulled out a pistol and shot you in the leg, and you then fell from your horse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then the Serbs from Cafe Srbija approached you and took you to hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That's a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, who took you to hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Who took me to hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: A Muslim with a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There weren't any Muslims nearby at the time, just the Serbs from Cafe Srbija.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: But I didn't come close, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, you did. Had there been firing from automatic weapons, no one would have approached me.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, I was between two lines of fire, and I crawled out by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were hit at a quarter past 8.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the skirmish between the Muslims and the Serbs began at 9.00?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That's when it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Forty-five minutes later?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, then who could have pulled you out of the crossfire?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I did that by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't do that. It was the Serbs who collected you and took you to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, you can't convince me of something that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the horse was not injured.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, the horse was injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a logical point of view, well, we can imagine, you are mounted on your horse, galloping fast, maybe - we don't know - and you're about to launch your hand-grenade. One of the Serbs, Mirko Blagojevic, shoots you and you fall off your horse. And if there is no one else, so you can very easily understand the reaction of the Serbs. They could have killed you immediately, or we don't know, because you were about to throw a hand-grenade. So there is a mystery there, because it seems that nothing is happening, and you tell us a Muslim brought you back. There might be another explanation. There may be shootings left and right between the Muslims and the Serbs, and you took advantage of this situation to flee and go to the hospital. Is this possible, is it not possible? I wasn't there. You were there. You're the only one who can tell us really what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to explain this to Mr. Seselj. When I was wounded, the Chetniks standing in front of Cafe Srbija were firing because they thought I would throw the hand-grenade. And when I came some 15 or 20 metres close to the cafe, they fired, and I fell from my horse. Then the Muslims from Cafe Istanbul also started firing, and I was caught in the crossfire, but I managed to crawl out on my own, and after that a Muslim took me to hospital. Mr. Seselj, on the other hand, claims that it was a Serb who took me to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The street between Cafe Istanbul and Cafe Srbija is quite narrow, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a normal width of street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it has a narrow pavement, there are two lanes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: There's a bus stop nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But not in that street?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, in that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Between Cafe Srbija and Cafe Istanbul, there's no bus stop?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is; all right. Do you know that this horse, some ten days later, was seen grazing in the nearby parks near the bus stop, the Cafe Srbija and so on, until someone took it away?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't see it. I didn't have an opportunity of seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that I learned about this event a few months later, and do you know that Mirko Blagojevic was one of the best marksmen in the former Yugoslavia, and his specialty was firing from a pistol?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, you're all specialists in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know about Mirko Blagojevic? Well, I'm very skillful in handling a gun, but a rifle -- that may be something you find amusing, but do you know that Mirko Blagojevic was one of the best marksmen from a pistol in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe because he's yours, you think he's always the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he always was one of the best men in Bijeljina. Are you aware that a few months later, when I learned of this event, I severely criticised Mirko Blagojevic, because when he saw you charging on a horse with a hand-grenade, he shot you in the leg, thus risking hitting the horse as well? I told him that he should have shot you in the head and then the horse would have been safe. Did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, but knowing you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection. It is inflammatory and Mr. Seselj has no -- that has no place in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's only evidence that you were in charge of all the events in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not -- Judges, this is not inflammatory. It's a fact which happened, and I might call Mirko Blagojevic as a witness in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then he will testify to all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a veiled threat and is inappropriate in this courtroom. It's inappropriate in general, but certainly in this courtroom and should not be tolerated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is no threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, I don't really understand your objection. Mr. Seselj recognises that he knew Mr. Blagojevic. That's the first thing. Secondly, he said that two months later he criticised Blagojevic, asking him -- telling him that -- asking him why he did not kill him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, that's an admission on my part. I think he should have killed a man charging at him with a hand-grenade, not shoot him in the leg and risk injuring the horse. So my reaction is quite normal. It would have been a pure self-defence -- a form of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Later, you said that when the conflict broke out, for the first three days the hospital was held by the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, for how many days did the conflict in Bijeljina continue?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, three days, around three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It may have been four?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it may have been four. I was in hospital the whole time, so I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it was only on the fourth day that the Serbs took over the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, the hospital was the last place to fall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is very valuable information, seen from the aspect of other witness testimony, because this witness says that the conflict lasted four days. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you were brought to hospital, you have an entry-exit wound, and you're bleeding; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the first thing they did in the hospital was to give you a drip. They were afraid you would bleed to death; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then they saw that the artery was not injured, and they dressed your wound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And after a while, the bleeding was staunched?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, not right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, when did the bleeding stop?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: A few hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A few hours later. And that first night, you had the drip; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the bleeding stopped, why would you still have a drip the next day? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I had lost a lot of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But why would you have a drip for three days? You had a normal meal, so you received food, water, teas and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I had lost too much blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you know what, I know a little about these things, and I have been given drips for 20 days at a time, you know. You arrived there, you lost a lot of blood, you were given a litre, two litres, or four litres of solution. Your wound was dealt with, the bleeding stopped. Why would the drip be kept for three days?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Ask Dr. Kicanovic and the other doctors that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay, I'll ask him. On the fourth day, as you say, Mirko Blagojevic arrived?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were still -- you still had the drip?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he then toppled over that drip thing?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you've made all this up, because on the fourth day you were no longer receiving a drip; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, what do you look at when you're lying down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at you. You did not have a drip at that time. Mirko Blagojevic did not come to see you in the hospital at all, he did not visit you at all, and you made up that he stabbed you with a bayonet where your wound was because you have no bayonet scars on your leg, or knife scars. You have only the traces of an entry-exit wound made by a pistol, and as the artery was not damaged at all, your wound needed only superficial treatment. And now show the bayonet traces here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Should I take my shoes off?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let Their Honours decide, but you have no traces left by a bayonet on your leg, no scars.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic was not in the hospital? You've got that written down as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to ask you to remove your clothes, to take off your clothes. If I were in my country, there would be no problems. You would be able to show your legs to everybody. But with the Rules we have here, it's far more complicated. You say that you have the trace of a bayonet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that you spent nine days in the hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So on the 31st, in the evening, you were taken to hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Before the 1st -- 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were there until the 9th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then you say that Arkan had you discharged from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We will have to wait for the Trial Chamber, because I think it is very important for them to also hear this. Does this mean that Arkan personally discharged the patients and the wounded from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But on the 9th of April, Arkan could not have been in Bijeljina at all, because already on the 7th of April, he had already been in Zvornik, and on the 8th of April, he personally participated in the battle for Zvornik. It is impossible for Arkan to have been in Bijeljina on the 9th of April, it is impossible.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you say that he personally, Arkan, that is, discharged you from hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: And Mirko -- in order for Mirko not to finish me off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So Arkan was saving you from Mirko. And we have hundreds of pieces of evidence to the effect that at that time, Arkan was fighting in Bijeljina. How can there be two Arkans, one in Bijeljina and one in Zvornik? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you just said something. You said that Arkan wanted to save you from Mirko Blagojevic. For what reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this one wanted to kill me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Arkan, being so kind, wanted to help everybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether he was good, whether he was kind. Why that criminal wanted to save me then, I have no idea. Whether these are their Chetnik games or what, I really can't say. I really don't know. To show his good face, like they have saved someone, and they have killed so many people on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had Mirko Blagojevic wanted to kill you, he could have done that on that day. If he stabbed you with a bayonet in your wound, in your leg, he could also have stabbed you in the heart.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: But according to him, I did not deserve to be killed quickly. I was to be tormented for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he was to stab you a little every day with a bayonet?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how many stabs did you get in total?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Just one. You want to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come, then, that he just stabbed you once and not -- during those days, and then Arkan concluded that you should be released, set free to go home?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, house the arrest, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you mean house the arrest? There were guards outside your house.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: There was guards. There was a garrison, in fact, outside my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it was important for Arkan for you to be released?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Not Arkan, but the White Eagles. Do you know who the White Eagles are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to -- where is the rationale there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't even go to the toilet, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I'm trying to see where is the rationale in what you are saying. This famous Srbija Cafe, where Arkan, if I got it correctly, used to meet with Mr. Seselj's men and other people, this cafe, according to what you said, was attacked by a person, you, yourself, who was mounted on a horse with a hand-grenade. I just imagine very well how the people in the cafe felt, knowing that you were going to throw a hand-grenade on the cafe. And all of a sudden, amongst all the people in this cafe, one comes to rescue you, Mr. Arkan, and the other one, Blagojevic, comes to bother you and to stab you with his bayonet? From a logical point of view, I have problems in understanding that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very good question. Nobody has asked me that. When I set out to throw the grenade, nobody asked me who it was that I wanted to throw the grenade at, who was down there in Srbija Cafe. Seselj's men, Arkan's men, and armed men, armed troops who were prepared to attack Bijeljina, to perpetrate crimes, were there, and the local, Mirko Blagojevic, I mean, his men. There were no civilians, there were no children, women. There were armed people down there, armed men from Serbia, and locals, and Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Mr. Witness. But if you did what you said, i.e., to throw a hand-grenade, these people may also want to take their revenge, including Arkan, who could also have been wounded by this grenade. But instead of that, he came to rescue you, and the other one came to bother you with his bayonet. That's where I have problems understanding, but everything is possible. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Arkan did not save me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Gusalic, you said that the cafe was full of Arkan's men, Seselj's men, Mirko's men, and troops?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that logical, for a significant military force to be concentrated in a cafe?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It is possible. You can see that it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is possible. According to my information, there were no Arkan's men in Bijeljina at all before the conflict broke out. It was only on the next day that Arkan came to Bijeljina, and he had a total of 30 men, including himself, and he joined in the fighting. So you made up that Arkan's men and Arkan had come before that, and you also invented that Arkan's men and Seselj's men were training people in Amajlije?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That is made up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. There were no Arkan's men, no Seselj's men, in Amajlije.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: And who was there, pray tell?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Sir, but you trained them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I trained them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Your men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My men trained the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I had the experts to train the Territorial Defence; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If that is what you think, you can testify according to what you feel is the truth.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Not what I -- no, it's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, if you say it's the truth. Secondly, during that conflict, within Bijeljina there were only Radical Party members from Bijeljina with weapons. Not a single member of the Serbian Radical Party from Serbia was there. This is what other Muslim witnesses have stated here.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That means --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But when Arkan came to Bijeljina on the 1st of April, he came to Dvorovi, where the Serbian Territorial Defence was concentrated, and from where it set out to clash with Muslim armed formations; whereas, in the centre of Bijeljina, the only resistance being offered to the Muslim forces was that by Serbian Radicals, led by Mirko Blagojevic, and there was nobody else there but the Serbian Radicals and Mirko Blagojevic. So you made it up that Arkan had been in Bijeljina at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, it is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fine, if it is not. You said that I, Arkan, and Mirko armed the Serbs. So where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: People said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where did we get the weapons?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who said so, the women in the barber shop?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, the women in the barber shop. People said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So people were saying that I, Arkan, and Mirko were arming the people?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, what we had contributed towards for 50 years, all of us together, the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you're talking about the JNA depots, and we took them over, according to you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: You took everything over. It was all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you. That is very interesting. Fine.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: You took it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that -- no, let's skip over this, because I have no reason to dwell on this. You said that later you were taken to Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: But you did not manage to perpetrate your ethnic combination [as interpreted], the one that you were bent on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Leave that aside. I'm not interested in that for now. You say that Serbs beat you in the Batkovic camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did the detained Muslim prisoners also beat you in the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Fikret Piklic, and Dzemal Zahirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Dzemal Zahirovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Piklic, Fikret?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did these two detained Muslims beat you? And they beat you viciously, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Not only me. They beat all the inmates in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Dzemal Zahirovic and Fikret, Piklic beat you up viciously because

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And because you assaulted a lad, the other Muslims beat you up; is that correct? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: What an animal you are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, don't you feel well? Do you need a break? Okay. So then we shall have a 20 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we resume, Mr. Seselj, and the Trial Chamber has decided to redact that part in the transcript where (redacted), and this has nothing to do with this case, and we will also redact the three sentences I have mentioned. Let us now bring in the witness. Could the usher go and bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, before the witness enters, will you allow me to comment on your decision on redacting this passage to express my opposition to that decision. Mr. President, this witness claims that in the Batkovic camp, he was systematically beaten by Serb soldiers and guards. That is not true. He was beaten almost to death by his compatriots there, also prisoners of the camp, for the reasons adduced here, and that basically refutes the veracity of his testimony. That is why I am against that being redacted or expunged from the transcript. If we are going to redact every detail, every bit of information which calls in question the veracity of the entire testimony, what's the point of cross-examination, then? But these are well-known facts. All the Muslims who were in that collection centre for prisoners or detention centre, they all know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we will move on to a private session for just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You spoke here about the food the prisoners in the Batkovic collection camp were given. You said that they gave you beans which had gone bad?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct that you received exactly the same food as the Serbian guards guarding you every day?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you got beans, did they get beans also?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, how should I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, did you see food being distributed to them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: How could I see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they eat there or did they go to eat somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: How would I know? I was imprisoned inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you were there; I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: But I was inside the hangar. How would I know what the Serbian soldiers were eating?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my information, the food prepared for you and for them was identical, and you'll recall that beans were the favourite food of soldiers in the former JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, normal beans.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, why would these be abnormal?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Because they would keep it there for ten days and then distribute it to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would they keep it for ten days?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: For it to go bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they did that on purpose?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they ever make you eat straw?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did you eat straw?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking for myself. They made me eat straw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about you. Did you eat it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I tried to, but I couldn't. It was very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how could they make you eat straw when we all know that it's not possible to eat straw? It's a bit odd.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It sounds odd. It's -- yeah, it's sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how much time did you spend in total in Batkovici and in Usora, near Doboj? When were you released from Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you spent more than a year and a half there, some of the time in Batkovici, some in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, 16 or 17 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there a Muslim who was there for longer than you were?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my information, no one was there for longer than you were. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible. Everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to the information I have --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: But I don't believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my information, which comes from Serb sources, the Serb authorities offered the Muslim authorities an exchange more than once, but the Muslim authorities refused to take you. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Because my side asked for me in every exchange. I was always near the top of the list, but you wouldn't let me be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How is it possible for other Muslim prisoners to spend two or three months there, at the most, with rare exceptions - only a few of them were there for longer than that - and you spent more than a year and a half there? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what prison inmate was there for only two or three months. They were all there for a year or so, or five or six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's not correct that they were there for a year. You said they came from all over the place?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, these are not just villages, these are towns and municipalities.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Both towns and municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vlasenica and Zvornik are towns?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they also came from the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Did the Muslim authorities hold it against you that by your impetuous throwing of a hand-grenade on Cafe Srbija, the conflict in Bijeljina started a few days earlier than planned?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the conflict had been planned for the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina was expected?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, that is what you planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was an order issued by Alija Izetbegovic that on that day, the take-over of the barracks and other facilities should begin?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a Muslim Crisis Staff of Bijeljina planning all this?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No. That's all lies, it's all lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's all lies, it didn't happen at all? Are you aware where the Muslims got automatic weapons from, and snipers?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the hunting rifles they had?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, my question is very precise, automatic rifles and snipers.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were the Muslims armed with those weapons?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't believe anyone had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know where Gvozdevic is?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Gvozdevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, Gvozdevic.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there a conflict there between -- among Muslims, between Muslims themselves, when some set out to wage war against the Serbs and others opposed this?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You're not aware of it. Are you aware -- were you given any medical examinations after you left Batkovici, after you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: In the Tuzla Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have the medical records from that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: With me, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not with you. Did you hand them over to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nobody asked you to? Did you state that, in fact, you never even visited a doctor after that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: You misread what I said. I said I had never been to see a doctor before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On page 8, in paragraph 3 from the bottom, the penultimate sentence or, rather, in this whole paragraph, you say that your left arm was broken in Batkovic, that three -- that your spine was damaged in three places, that you had a scar from an iron that was pressed against your arm, that you had injuries on your chest, that you had several bones broken, and that you had scars from cuts on your skull, and you say you don't know that your skull was broken. And you say after that, I never visited a doctor. And now it turns out that you were examined in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was examined then and also in 2004, in Tuzla, when there was a trial. That was when a doctor examined me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And The Hague investigators never asked to see your medical records?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. It all has to be -- it can all be proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know it can all be proved if there are documents available.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't doubt it. In my view, you here are an impersonation of international justice. You are what international justice relies on, so when I imagine international justice, I see your face. What I am interested in is why the OTP did not ask to see your medical records. Did you find this strange?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't find it strange. Why should I find it strange if I feel well?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's not about how you feel now, but what you looked like immediately after leaving the Batkovici Collection Centre. Your entries were then fresh, and medical documentation might corroborate your statement, if your statement is true; is that correct? And then I could not object to anything; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Muslims authorities hold it against you that you made a statement for Serbian TV while you were in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Why would they hold it against me? They knew why I was making statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, why?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Because I was forced to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They forced you to make statements for TV Bijeljina five times?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count, but it was more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, here on page 10 you say "about five times"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: And for some Russians and I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, why would they choose you of all people to make those statements?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were more eminent people in Batkovici; right? Muslim political leaders, and military leaders, and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to inmates?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm referring to prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were more eminent people than you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: But the ten of us were special.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would they select you, of all people, to give statements five times for TV Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably made others do it as well, those eminent people you're mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hear on TV Bijeljina that Muslims from Batkovici kept appearing. Why would they choose you, of all people, if you constantly had wounds and scars and bruises from beatings? Wouldn't that be odd?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if in the Batkovic Collection Centre you were constantly beaten and maltreated --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This left traces on your head, face, hands and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, then, would you be suitable for showing on television, for Serbian propaganda, that Batkovic is a nice place, that the Muslims are responsible for the war, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like a hidden camera, and they made me talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't know they were filming you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they were filming me or not. Maybe they weren't. They made me talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They took you to the TV station in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: A newspaperman, TV crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they take you to the TV?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, radio, television, I don't know. They did film me or record me. Whether it was a TV or something, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, explain this to me. Newspapermen arrived in Batkovici, journalists; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they chose you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: There were people with ties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they selected you and took you to Bijeljina, to the television station?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honours. I'm just trying to understand if Mr. Seselj is speaking of the first Batkovic detention or the second one, after Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you went to do the TV in Bijeljina, was it the first time or the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it the first time or the second time, Mr. Witness, because your answer was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second time, okay. So, Mr. Witness, I'm a judge who is wondering. I'm not here to consider that what the Prosecutor or Defence says is necessarily the truth. I'm just trying to understand what is the rationale or the logic in what I hear the witness say. Maybe the Prosecution or the Defence might not like it, but I'm just doing my job. If you were beaten, as you say, with all the wounds you mentioned which have been seen by the judge in Tuzla, who did his job properly by asking for some medical examination, how come the authorities of the camp selected you to speak before the TV, while you could have said to everybody, Well, this is what happened to me? Do you have an answer to this question? Because this is something you may ask yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need a second. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat slowly my question. You said you were beaten in the Batkovic camp. That, we understood. And we know that you went to the TV stations. I would like to understand how someone who has been beaten, someone who has wounds and traces, may be shown on TV. That's what I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it was a TV crew and whether they were filming me for TV directly, but I went to all their interrogations to say how I started the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you told them what happened to you, you told them you had been beaten, or did you not say anything? And one may understand if you did not say anything, because you were a prisoner. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But -- but to whom could I say something when it was all the same? The Serbian Republic was taking me to the Serbian journalists. It was all under their authority, so what could I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you make a statement for a foreign TV crew?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That was the first time I was in Batkovic, the first three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the first three months. What country were these foreigners from?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I think they were Russians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: It was in the village of Trnovo, not in Bijeljina. They took us outside Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you tell them that you had been beaten in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, who could I tell?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the journalists, you could tell the journalists. The foreign journalists, you could have told them, whether they were Russian or from somewhere else. That would have been an occasion for you to say, I'm being beaten here. The journalists would have done their job professionally, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, how do I know who comes from where and who's what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they were foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I was a prisoner, I was beaten, and you expect me to say that I'm being beaten while I'm still a prisoner? Who would have the courage to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, explain this to me: In those first three months, that was when you got the most beatings?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were all wounded?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Those first three months, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And full of bruises?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So why would they choose you, of all people, to show to a foreign TV crew?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, they had a go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For you to say that you had not been beaten, and people can see you're covered in bruises?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, they dressed me up. I was nicely dressed, as I am now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they beat you on the head as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, explain how they beat you with a five- or six-kilo stone or rock. You say they hit you with chains, with rods, with hoe handles, and with a five- or six-kilo stone. What did this look like?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, a small man, he was short, he couldn't reach me, so I had to kneel down for him to be able to hit me, and there's an eight-inch-long scar, a long scar, and a lot of small scars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So let's be patient about this. This is a small man, holding a five- to six-kilogram stone?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Exactly. This is a stone from the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it is like we use for sauerkraut, and he's holding you with two hands?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he cannot hold it in one hand only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he told you to kneel?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then when you knelt, he hit you on the head with it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many hits, with such a big stone, can one take on the head without actually dying?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, the man -- man is the biggest animal, and he can take a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you called me an animal a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in this particular case, I was referring to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he was hitting you. And did he continue to hold this stone in his hand?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So a second time, a third time, this five- to six-kilogram stone?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I didn't count the number of hits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many could there have been?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, you count. You think about it. How many could you take?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I think my skull would have been fractured with the first hit, although my head is the strongest in Scheveningen.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Well, it is not stronger than mine, it is not tougher than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
